sentences.text: The piopio was an extinct genus of passerine birds found only in New Zealand.
Although sometimes called New Zealand thrushes, the piopio only superficially resembled the thrush family.
The South Island piopio was last recorded in 1905.
The species name Turnagra tanagra was based on a mistaken belief that the bird was related to American tanagers.
The piopio frequented the undergrowth and forest floor.
The piopio built well-constructed cup nests in trees a few meters off the ground, laying two to four eggs.
The piopio were omnivorous, eating insects, spiders, fruit, and oats.
The genus Turnagra was placed in the family Oriolidae because the birds were closely related to figbirds.
The piopio were split into separate North Island and South Island species in 2012.
The piopio lived during the Holocene epoch.
The genus Turnagra existed from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
Some researchers have suggested a relationship between the piopio and the whistler family (Pachycephalidae).
